meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals
meta.pedagogy: Hands-on learning with step-by-step guidance. Each exercise builds on the previous. All concepts from the session are coded. Banking/finance examples used for context.

objectives: Implement all flow control structures (if/else, switch, for, while, do-while, break, continue) in a realistic ATM simulation.
prerequisites: IntelliJ IDEA (Community Edition) or VS Code with Java Extension
Git installed and GitHub account created

exercises.title: Flow Control — ATM Simulator
exercises.objective: Implement all flow control structures (if/else, switch, for, while, do-while, break, continue) in a realistic ATM simulation.
exercises.scenario: Build a simplified ATM simulator for RoboBank. It validates PIN (do-while), processes transactions (switch), handles withdrawals (if/else), and generates a mini-statement (for loop).
instructions: Step 1: Create class 'ATMSimulator' and type the starter code
Step 2: Complete all TODO sections — do NOT skip any
Step 3: Run with the test data provided (pinAttempts array simulates user input)
Step 4: Change the test data to test edge cases: wrong PIN 3 times, insufficient balance, zero amount
Step 5: Add a new transaction type: 'B' for Balance Inquiry (print the balance)
Step 6: CHALLENGE: Add a minimum balance check — don't allow withdrawal if balance would go below ₹1000

hints: do-while checks condition AFTER the body — guarantees at least one execution. Perfect for 'show prompt, then validate' patterns.
switch falls through unless you use break. In our switch: break exits the switch; to exit the outer for loop from inside case 'Q', use a boolean flag: boolean quit = false; then check while (!quit).
Math.abs(-5000) = 5000. Useful for converting negative debit amounts to positive for display.
reflection_questions: Why is do-while more appropriate than while for the PIN authentication loop?
What would happen with 'break' inside the switch case 'Q' — does it exit the for loop or just the switch?
Can you rewrite the for-each loop in Section 3 as a traditional for loop? Which is cleaner?
exercises.debugging_task: Add this code and observe: simulate a card being blocked. Set simulatedPINs = {9999, 8888, 7777} (all wrong). Does your card-blocked logic trigger? What output do you see?
